the proper lumping technique can be applied to a complex systems pharmacology model to reduce its complexity, resulting in a simplified model with the same mechanistic basis.

the development of a systems pharmacokinetics–systems pharmacodynamics model to describe the time course of the recovery of fibrinogen after a brown snake venom bite.
the development and application of a systems pharmacokinetics–systems pharmacodynamics model to the description of the pharmacokinetics– pharmacodynamics of the venom–fibrinsogen relationship.

the development of a systems pharmacological model of the co-agulation network that can be used for the description of the time course of recovery of fibrinogen concentration after brown snake venom exposure.

the proposed technique is an effective tool for reducing the number of states in a complex system model while retaining the essential dynamics of the original system.
a 62‐state model of coagulation can be simplified to a 5 ‐state model that is sufficient to describe the time course of recovery of fibrinogen after a snake venom exposure.

the proposed model is an appropriate representation of the coagulant venom–fibrinsogen interaction and that this model is suitable for the purpose for which it was developed, i.e. the description of the decline and recovery of plasma fibrinogen after a brown snake (Pseudechis australis) bite.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a systems pharmacology approach can be used to describe pharmacokinetic–pharmacodynamic relationships, and that a simplified model can be developed from the original model by using the technique of proper lumpings.
a systems pharmacology approach can be used to model the decline in fibrinogen after a snake bite and the subsequent recovery.
we developed a simplified model that describes the time‐dependent decline and recovery in the fibrinogen concentration after a brown snake venom injection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the simplification of complex models is possible and can be achieved by using the proper lumping technique.
the complexity of systems biology models can be reduced by identifying states that are not relevant to a particular input–output relationship and eliminating them from the model.
it is possible to reduce a complex model to one of a more manageable size while maintaining a mechanistic relationship.
